System design · Module 03 of 29 · Level 1: Foundations

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

Before choosing a database or adding a cache, you need to know roughly how much traffic and data you're dealing with. Not to the last request: to the nearest power of ten. Ten minutes of rounded arithmetic tells you whether one server is plenty or whether you need a fleet, and it stops you building machinery a problem doesn't need.

1. The idea

Planning a party for 60 people, you don't count slices. You think: about three slices each, eight slices a pizza, so roughly 20–25 pizzas, and one oven can't bake that in an hour, so order from two shops. Rough numbers, one clear decision. That's a back-of-the-envelope estimate.

An estimate turns a vague description ("a photo app for 50 million people") into four numbers that drive design decisions:

  1. Requests per second, on average and at peak, split into reads and writes. This decides how many servers, and whether you need a cache.
  2. Storage per day and over the data's lifetime. This decides whether one database fits, and where big files go.
  3. Bandwidth: bytes per second going out to users. This decides whether you need a CDN.
  4. Memory for the hot data. This decides whether the working set fits in one cache.

The trick that makes it fast: round everything to one significant figure and work in powers of ten. A day has 86,400 seconds; call it 105. You'll be off by about 15%, which never changes a design decision.

PowerCountBytesHandy facts
103thousandKBA short text record with a few fields: hundreds of bytes to ~1 KB
106millionMBA phone photo: ~2–5 MB original, ~100–300 KB resized for display
109billionGBA minute of 1080p video streamed at 5 Mbit/s: ~40 MB
1012trillionTBA large single database: tens of TB
1015quadrillionPBBig video and photo platforms store many PB in blob storage

Time conversions to know by heart: 1 day ≈ 105 s · 1 month ≈ 2.5 × 106 s · 1 year ≈ 3 × 107 s. So 1 million per day ≈ 12 per second, and 1 billion per day ≈ 12,000 per second.

2. How it works

The same recipe works for almost any system. Press Play to watch it on a photo-sharing app with 50 million daily active users.

Every line ended in a decisionThat's the point. "29,000 reads per second" is trivia; "so we need a cache in front of the database" is design. If a number wouldn't change what you build, you don't need to calculate it.

The recipe

  1. Users: daily active users (DAU). If you're given monthly users, DAU is often 20–50% of that.
  2. Actions: reads and writes per user per day. Most products are read-heavy: 10:1 to 100:1.
  3. Per second: per day ÷ 105.
  4. Peak: × 2–3 for a normal daily peak; × 10 or more for launches, sales and live events.
  5. Storage: writes per day × bytes each × days kept. Multiply by about 3 for replicas, and add room for indexes.
  6. Bandwidth: read QPS × response size. Watch bits vs bytes: 1 GB/s = 8 Gbit/s.
  7. Verdict: compare each number with what one machine can do (Module 02) and say what it means for the design.

Conversion drill

Speed comes from practice. Answer in your head, then reveal. Aim for the right power of ten in under ten seconds.

4. Trade-offs

Speed over precision

One significant figure is enough. Spending ten minutes getting 11,574 instead of "about 10,000" costs you time and changes nothing.

State your assumptions

"I'll assume 50M daily users, each viewing 50 photos." Saying it lets others correct you early, and makes the result easy to redo when the assumption changes.

Only calculate what decides something

In an interview, skip a long estimate up front. Do the math at the moment it matters: "Does the top-K fit in one machine's memory? 10M items × 100 bytes = 1 GB, yes."

Peak and growth, not just today

Systems fail at peak, not on average, and data only grows. Estimate the peak, and the size in a few years, before deciding one machine is enough.

5. In real systems

At work, the same arithmetic becomes capacity planning:

  • Start with an estimate, then measure. A load test (with tools such as k6, Locust, Gatling or JMeter) tells you what one server really handles for your requests. The estimate tells you how many of those you'll need.
  • Plan for peaks and failures. Size so that at peak, with one server or one zone lost, the rest still run below ~70% (Module 02's headroom).
  • Watch the growth curve. Storage grows every day; requests grow with users. A design that fits today but hits a limit in 18 months needs a plan now, not code now.
  • Estimate cost the same way. Instance-hours, GB stored and GB transferred out, each times a price from the provider's pricing page. Data transfer out to the internet and cross-region traffic are the costs people most often forget.

Sizes worth memorising: an ID or timestamp 8 bytes; a UUID 16 bytes (36 as text); a typical row of user content a few hundred bytes to 1 KB; a resized image 100–300 KB; video at a few Mbit/s, or tens of MB per minute.

6. Remember it

Memory hook: "A day is a hundred thousand seconds"Per day ÷ 10⁵ = per second. Then × peak, × bytes, and finish every number with "so we need…".
How this hook works: what "A day is a hundred thousand seconds" means

What the slogan means

"A day"
Products are described per day (users, posts, views), but servers are sized per second. The day is the bridge.
"a hundred thousand seconds"
86,400 rounded to 10⁵. Dividing by a power of ten is something you can do instantly in your head: 3 billion a day is 30,000 a second.
(and what it implies)
The rounding is deliberate. Estimates aim for the right power of ten, not the right digits.

Why this picture fits: it's the one conversion you'll use in every estimate, and it carries the whole method in it: round boldly, convert, then decide.

The story → the concept

StepWhat you write
Per dayDAU × actions per user
÷ a hundred thousandAverage per second
× peak factorThe number you size for
× bytes × daysStorage and bandwidth
"so we need…"The design decision

Watch it on an example

A chat app: 200M daily users, each sending 40 messages a day.

  1. Per day: 200M × 40 = 8 × 10⁹ messages.
  2. ÷ 10⁵ = 80,000 messages per second on average; × 3 at peak ≈ 250,000 per second.
  3. × 200 bytes ≈ 1.6 TB of new messages a day; ≈ 600 TB a year before replication.
  4. So we need: a write-optimised store split across many machines, and connection servers for the live traffic. One relational database won't do.

The trap it saves you from

Either extreme: designing a planet-scale system for 10,000 users, or putting 250,000 writes per second on one database. Ten seconds of arithmetic tells you which world you're in.

It still works when…

The unit isn't requests: GPU-seconds per day for an AI feature, emails per day, sensor readings per day. Per day ÷ 10⁵ still gets you to "per second", which is what machines are sized by.

7. Common mistakes

Estimating without concludingA page of numbers that doesn't end in "so we need X" or "so one database is fine" has wasted the time. Every number should change or confirm a decision.
Sizing for the averageTraffic peaks at 2–3× the daily average, and much more during events. Size for the peak.
Mixing up bits and bytesNetwork speeds are in bits (Gbit/s), storage in bytes (GB). 1 GB/s of video out is 8 Gbit/s of network.
Forgetting replicas, indexes and metadataRaw data × 3 replicas, plus indexes, plus backups, is easily 4–5× the raw number.
False precision"11,574.07 requests per second" suggests accuracy the inputs don't have. Say "about 10,000" and move on.

8. Design exercise (25 minutes)

  1. URL shortener. 100M new links a month, read 100 times each on average, kept for 10 years, ~500 bytes per link. Estimate write QPS, read QPS at peak, and total storage. Does it fit one database?
  2. Ride hailing. 5M drivers online at peak, each sending a location every 4 seconds. Estimate writes per second. What does that number rule out?
  3. Video platform. 500 hours of video uploaded per minute, stored in 4 resolutions averaging 1 GB per hour each. Estimate storage per day and per year.
  4. Check yourself. Put each into the calculator above (adjust the presets) and compare.
  5. Write it down. In your design notebook: the three conversions (day, month, year) and the bits/bytes rule.

9. Self-check quiz

About how many requests per second is 1 billion requests per day?

10⁹ ÷ 10⁵ = 10⁴. The exact figure is 11,574, but "about 10,000" leads to the same design.

A service sends 10 GB per second to users. What network capacity is that?

Multiply bytes by 8 for bits: 10 GB/s = 80 Gbit/s. That's a strong hint you need a CDN.

When is it worth doing an estimate in an interview?

Do the math at the moment it decides something: whether data fits in memory, whether one database can take the writes.

What should you size servers for?

Failures happen at peak. Size for peak load running at ~50–70% utilization, so you can absorb spikes and lose a machine.
